item.title: Websites taken down worldwide as critical cyber-security update issued
item.description:
Image source, Getty ImagesByTom Gerken and Laura Cress, Technology reporters and Joe Tidy, Cyber correspondent, BBC World ServicePublished21 October 2026
International governments and agencies have urged websites to address two critical cyber-security flaws in a programming language which powers much of the internet.
The vulnerabilities were found within the PHP programming language, with a fix issued on Wednesday afternoon.
Multiple cyber-security agencies have urged organisations unable to apply fixes in time to consider taking their sites down, leaving bodies such as the Finnish government, Edinburgh council and the BBC to take pages offline.
The flaws were discovered by AI, with cyber-security firm Wiz saying they were the "most severe vulnerabilities ever discovered" by the tech, which is reshaping the cyber landscape.
Finland has temporarily shut down the government's public web services, while the Netherlands' cyber-security agency said it was taking its own website offline due to the vulnerabilities.
The US National Security Agency issued similar advice on X, external for organisations to take their systems offline if they were unable to update with the fix.
"These vulnerabilities often provide a direct path to the server's file system or database," it wrote.
Meanwhile, the White House said federal agencies were working with leading AI labs to speed up a fix to the issue.
And in a post on X, external, Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi urged people to check if their publicly available websites ran on PHP.
The Wikimedia Foundation, which runs the online encyclopedia Wikipedia, said it was addressing the security vulnerabilities.
"We have taken down a number of other systems as a precautionary measure until they can be safely patched," it said.
That led some people to be unable to access parts of Wikipedia on Wednesday.

item.title: What is PHP and why did it spark a global cyber-security scramble?
item.description:
Image source, ReutersByOsmond ChiaBusiness reporterPublished1 hour ago
For more than a decade, serious flaws had gone undetected in technology underpinning much of the internet.
It took artificial intelligence (AI) to bring them to light and caused a global cyber-security alert.
The vulnerabilities lie within a programming language called PHP, which has been used internationally since the 2000s to build websites.
Governments and cyber-security agencies around the world scrambled to contain the fallout of this discovery on Wednesday, and have urged website operators to install a new emergency fix or consider taking their platforms offline.
Cyber-security firm Wiz - one of the companies whose researchers uncovered the vulnerabilities - described the flaws as the "most severe" ever detected by AI.
OpenAI, whose technology was used to find the flaws, called the discovery "one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory".
What is the flaw?
Most people may not have heard of PHP - short for PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor - but they most certainly interact with it daily.
PHP powers a vast number of platforms, including online shops, Wikipedia and WordPress – the content management system behind many websites like blogs.
When you visit a website like Wikipedia, PHP is the code that collects information you need and presents it in a way you can read on the web, Paul Spain, chief executive of Gorilla Cyber Security, told the BBC.
But due to a flaw that could allow attackers to take control of affected web servers without authentication and steal sensitive data, everything built on PHP was left exposed.
AI could make such attacks easier and faster, Spain said, estimating that the flaw could affect "millions and millions" of websites.
It would be "disastrous" if hackers or countries weaponised the flaw and seized private data from websites, said cyber-security researcher Jill Slay from the University of Adelaide.

item.title: Missiles hit Kyiv after Russia agrees to US call to resume Ukraine peace talks
item.description:
Image source, ReutersImage caption,
Russia has in recent weeks intensified its deadly missile and drone attacks on Kyiv and other Ukrainian citiesByJaroslav LukivPublished21 October 2026
Ukraine's capital has come under a new missile attack, hours after Russia said it was "ready in principle" to resume peace talks and the US president said the world was "the closest we've been" to ending the war.
Several houses were hit on Wednesday night, injuring six people, Kyiv Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko said.
The attack came amid a new diplomatic push led by Donald Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. Witkoff met Russia's President Vladimir Putin in the city of St Petersburg on Wednesday - a day after meeting Ukraine's leader.
Three-way talks were paused in February, after which Russia stepped up attacks as Ukraine ran out of Western-supplied interceptors to defend against missiles.
Speaking on Wednesday, Trump said: "The other day I was talking to Vladimir Putin about settling his war with Ukraine, which I think we're getting closer to, by the way, maybe now the closest we've been."
The US president has so far failed to bring the Russia-Ukraine war to an end despite his repeated comments that he would be able to achieve this.

Published9 hours ago
Trump's special envoy Witkoff went to St Petersburg after meeting Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky as well as the leaders of Norway and Finland in the Norwegian capital, Oslo, on Tuesday.
It is not clear what specific proposals Witkoff brought to Putin, but Zelensky said after the talks that "strong" security guarantees for Ukraine and energy ceasefire proposals had been discussed.
Putin's aide Yuri Ushakov said their ideas were not very "useful".
Top officials from Russia, Ukraine and the US have held several rounds of talks aimed at ending the war.

item.title: Rosenberg: US diplomatic push offers little hope for imminent Ukraine peace
item.description:
Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption,
Witkoff (R) said there was still important work to do after the meeting with Putin (L)BySteve RosenbergRussia Editor, Reporting fromMoscowPublished9 hours ago
After two days of diplomacy – in Norway's capital and Russia's St Petersburg – is the war in Ukraine any closer to ending?
"Good and constructive" is how Norway's prime minister described Tuesday's talks between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, US President Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff and European representatives.
In Oslo, the idea of a trilateral meeting at leaders' level was floated. The hope was that Steve Witkoff's trip to Russia would pave the way for President Vladimir Putin, Zelensky and Trump to meet and agree an end to the fighting.
But Putin has shown little desire to share a table with Zelensky - unless that table is in Moscow.
The Kremlin says it may be willing to resume trilateral talks next month in Abu Dhabi, but only at the technical level.
In a post on X, Steve Witkoff himself conceded that "there is still important work to do", though he claimed "President Trump remains committed to seeing this war end..."

item.title: US orders some diplomats to leave Saudi Arabia as Houthi attacks escalate
item.description:
Image source, ReutersImage caption,
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis also attacked the airport in Saudi Arabia's capital Riyadh earlier this monthByToby MannPublished4 hours ago
The US State Department has ordered some diplomats and their families to leave Saudi Arabia as attacks escalate, with three people killed in strikes across the country.
Saudi authorities said debris from a drone intercepted during an attempted attack on an oil field killed two people, while one person died after a strike at the King Fahd International Airport in Dammam.
Conflict between Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis and Saudi Arabia has been rising in the past month.
The Houthis have responded to Saudi strikes by launching missiles and drones at airports, energy facilities and military bases in Saudi Arabia. A recent strike on Riyadh's international airport was the deadliest in the kingdom in years.

"The US Department of State issued an ordered departure for non-emergency US government employees and their family members in Saudi Arabia," a state department spokesperson said in a statement.
"Iranian-supported Houthis have increasingly engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions," it added.
The spokesperson also warned "the hostilities have the potential to escalate rapidly".
In the latest attack on the King Fahd International Airport eight people sustained injuries that ranged from "minor to serious", officials said.
No details of the attack have yet been given, but the strike comes after airports in Saudi Arabia have been repeatedly targeted by Houthi forces.

item.title: Airbnb hosts can no longer make guests strip beds and wash dishes under new rules
item.description:
Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption,
Washing and putting away dishes are examples of chores that Airbnb says guests should generally not be asked to doBySareen HabeshianPublished6 hours ago
Airbnb has changed its rules to limit what property hosts may ask guests to do - including when it comes to cleaning.
The updated guidelines state that hosts can now set seven standard house rules and can also add other "reasonable" requests.
Airbnb states that guests - who are required to pay a cleaning fee - should not be asked to complete tasks normally done by a cleaner, including washing dishes and stripping beds.
The new rules will apply to all reservations booked on or after 20 November on the accommodation marketplace.
"House rules help guests understand what hosts expect, but we've heard from our community that they can be confusing, onerous and hard to manage," Airbnb told the BBC.
"So, we've redesigned them to make them easier to discover and clearer to set, alongside a new policy that keeps requests reasonable, with no surprises."
According to the new requirements on the Airbnb website, hosts are generally not allowed to ask guests to complete tasks that "require significant effort or time, or would typically be performed by a cleaner, including stripping the bed, taking trash offsite, or washing and putting away dishes".
The company said it may grant exceptions in some circumstances. For example, guests can be asked to limit shower time if there are local drought-related water restrictions.
A property's rules will be displayed to guests more prominently moving forward and will appear in the guests' reservation reminders.
Contracts will only be allowed in limited circumstances, including when required by law or homeowners association rules.
While a host will not be able to impose fines, they remain in control of their house rules and requests, the company said.

item.title: Macron accuses foreign leaders of exploiting French riots
item.description:
Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption,
Protesters rallied in Lille along with other cities across the countryByPatrick Jackson, Marco Silva and Thomas Copeland, BBC Verify Published21 October 2026
French President Emmanuel Macron has accused foreign leaders of exploiting the riots which erupted across the country on Saturday for electoral purposes.
Without naming them, he said they were campaigning for forthcoming elections "at France's expense" with their comments on the violence, which erupted on the fringe of cost-of-living protests.
Speaking on a visit to the Middle East, he referred to them as "leaders who are in campaign mode, whether here in the region or on the other side of the Atlantic".
It was an apparent swipe at Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who faces parliamentary elections next week, and US President Donald Trump, for whom mid-term polls fall next month.
Macron said the unnamed leaders had been influenced by fake videos generated by AI about the riots.
Nearly 150 people have been jailed and more than 800 brought before the courts since the riots which gripped Paris and other cities including Lyon, Marseille and Nice.
Video of running battles between masked rioters and police, as well as property being destroyed and stores being looted, spread across social media.
The government admitted the police had "lost control" during the violence, which came after weeks of protests by students over conditions in high schools.
Macron vowed afterwards that the authorities would be "uncompromising" towards "agitators from ultra-left fringe groups", which he blamed for much of the trouble.

item.title: No purchase, no seats: Starbucks China rolls out new policy
item.description:
Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption,
"Purchase to sit" signs are popping up in Starbucks stores around ChinaByKoh EwePublished1 hour ago
Taking a seat at a Starbucks in China? Just make sure you're also ordering something there.
A new policy by Starbucks China takes effect across all its 8,000 stores on Thursday, making it mandatory for people to purchase items if they want to sit in its cafes.
Starbucks China said the move was part of efforts to improve the "in-store experience" for customers. The company is facing stiff competition from homegrown brands such as Luckin Coffee.
Reports of the new policy circulated this week, along with social media videos of what appear to be "purchase to sit" signs in Starbucks stores.
Many on Chinese social media welcomed the new policy.
"Finally, there won't be peak periods where people are just sitting there not ordering anything, drinking Luckin coffee, playing games and yelling on the phone," reads one of the top-liked comment on Weibo. "Every time I walk around, there's nowhere to sit,"
"There's nothing wrong with it. I'd feel awkward sitting there if I didn't make a purchase. I'd rather leave the seats for those who made purchases and need the seats," another Weibo user commented.
Starbucks stores around the world have been wrestling with non-paying seat-hoggers and other undesirable behaviour from customers.
Last month, a Starbucks store in Sichuan province sparked debate after video of its chained-up outdoor seats and tables were circulated on social media. It appeared to be an attempt to block people from sitting there without paying.
In South Korea, Starbucks has told customers to stop bringing "bulky items" into their stores, after some patrons reportedly hogged seats with printers and desktop computers in tow.

item.title: US embassy accuses Canada of election meddling ahead of midterms
item.description:
Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption,
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, right, and Ontario Premier Doug Ford deny that their country is interfering in the US midterm electionsByNardine SaadPublished2 hours ago
The US Embassy in Ottawa has accused Canadian officials of election meddling ahead of the November midterms.
The embassy said Canadian leaders have brushed off concerns over "potential interference", and that ministers and premiers "openly describe plans to influence American politics in official documents and public appearances".
Canadian leaders, including Prime Minister Mark Carney, have dismissed the claims. Relations between the North American neighbours have hardened during second Trump administration.
The midterms will determine which political party controls both branches of the US Congress, which could have a significant impact on the rest of Donald Trump's presidency.
The fact sheet released by the US Embassy on Wednesday alleges the Canadian government "brushes off concerns about potential interference in U.S. elections, even as its ministers and premiers openly describe plans to influence American politics in official documents and public appearances".
It cites comments and actions, like meetings with US Democrats and calling for retaliatory tariffs against the US.
For example, it says that when Industry Minister Mélanie Joly was asked what she expected regarding tariffs if Democrats were to win midterm elections, she responded, "That's exactly why I'm meeting so many governors and potential presidential candidates."
Ontario Premier Doug Ford pushed Canada's federal government, it states, to consider additional retaliatory tariffs on imports from "politically significant states to the current administration's base of support".
Asked on Wednesday about the allegations, Carney noted that it was the US that first initiated trade actions against Canada.

item.title: New Mexico sues Epstein lawyer and accountant, accusing them of hiding his sex crimes
item.description:
Image source, ReutersImage caption,
Prosecutors say Epstein abused victims at his Zorro Ranch in New Mexico with the help of key aidesByMax MatzaPublished6 hours ago
Prosecutors in the US state of New Mexico have filed a civil lawsuit against two longtime aides of Jeffrey Epstein, accusing the men of profiting from the late financier's sex trafficking ring.
Lawyer Darren Indyke and accountant Richard Kahn are the sole executors of Epstein's estate, controlling all his wealth and possessions. They have denied any role in his crimes.
New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez says they played a key role in concealing abuse at Epstein's remote Zorro Ranch near the city of Santa Fe, and that they continue to earn money while victims seek accountability.
The lawsuit is separate to the state's ongoing criminal probe into Epstein, which was re-launched in February.
An attorney representing both Indyke and Kahn told the BBC that they "emphatically reject" the claims in the lawsuit.
The lawsuit was filed in New Mexico on Wednesday under the federal Trafficking Victims Protection Act and New Mexico Racketeering Act.
During a news conference, Torrez argued that the two men are blocking efforts by Epstein's victims to seek compensation from his fortune, estimated at roughly $635m (£474m) at the time of his death.
"Those resources rightfully belong in the hands of survivors - there should be no distribution of Mr Epstein's remaining assets to people like Mr Indyke and Mr Kahn for participation in what I think is one of the most horrific criminal enterprises in modern America," he said.
Both men worked with Epstein for decades, and have previously testified to Congress that they were unaware of the crimes he committed alongside accomplice Ghislane Maxwell.
Their attorney Daniel Weiner said in a statement to the BBC that, "they are confident that they will prevail on the claims asserted against them".
